opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that you can't really judge synthetic data by looking at it. A lot of people start by asking whether it looks good: is it fluent, is it diverse, would a human annotator rate it highly? Those things matter a little, but they're weak proxies. The real question is what the data does to the model once it's trained on it.

So I'd frame it in three layers.

**First, marginal contribution.** Hold everything else fixed, add or swap in the synthetic data, and measure the change on the capabilities you care about. That sounds obvious, but people often skip it because it's expensive. Without that ablation you're mostly guessing. And it has to be marginal: a dataset that helps a weak model can do nothing for a strong one that already knows those patterns. Value is always relative to what the model already has.

**Second, whether it adds information or just reshapes it.** A lot of synthetic data is the model, or a sibling model, restating what it already knows. That can still help: it can fix formatting, sharpen instruction-following, or make latent knowledge easier to access. But it's a different kind of value from data that brings genuinely new signal. The most valuable synthetic data usually has some external grounding injected somewhere. That might be a verifier, a compiler, a math checker, an environment, or real documents it was derived from. If there's no source of truth anywhere in the pipeline, I get suspicious, because you risk a closed loop where the model just amplifies its own biases and errors.

**Third, side effects.** You have to look beyond the target benchmark. Did diversity collapse? Did the outputs get more templated and more sycophantic? Did calibration get worse, so the model is now confidently wrong more often? Did some other capability quietly regress? Synthetic data is very good at moving one number up while degrading things you weren't measuring. I'd also watch the scaling behavior. If doubling the synthetic data gives you nothing, or makes things worse, that tells you it's saturated or that its distribution is too narrow.

And one practical point: be very careful about contamination and about "teaching to the test." When you generate data with a strong model, it's easy to end up producing things that look a lot like your eval set. Then you think the data is valuable when you've really just leaked the benchmark. So I'd want held-out evaluations built independently of the generation process.

So in one sentence: synthetic data is valuable to the degree that it gives the model verifiable signal it didn't already have, without narrowing the distribution, and the only real way to know is careful controlled training experiments, not inspecting the data itself.

r001.rationale: It contrasts judging whether synthetic data looks good with measuring what it does to the model after training.

r002.rationale: It discusses adding new or verifiable information, but does not identify increasing information density as a way to give models more value from less data.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think a lot of people get backwards. The instinct is to evaluate synthetic data the way you'd evaluate a product: is it realistic, is it diverse, does it pass some quality filter. But none of that is actually the question. The only thing that matters is whether the model gets better after training on it, and better at what you care about, not better at reproducing the synthetic data itself.

So the first principle I'd offer is that synthetic data has no intrinsic value. Its value is entirely conditional on the model you're feeding it to. The same dataset can be enormously useful for a small model and nearly worthless for a frontier one, because what it's really providing is information the model doesn't already have. If the generator and the student know roughly the same things, you're mostly just recycling.

That leads to how I'd actually measure it. You hold out an evaluation set that is as far from the synthetic generation process as you can make it. Real user queries, real failures, tasks collected independently. Then you do controlled ablations: train with and without the synthetic slice, keeping everything else fixed, and look at the delta on that held-out set. If you only evaluate on benchmarks that resemble your synthetic data, you'll fool yourself every time. The model will look wonderful on the distribution you generated and quietly regress elsewhere.

The second thing I'd watch is the cost side of the ledger. Synthetic data is cheap to produce in volume, so people flood the training mix with it, and then capacity gets spent on the synthetic distribution at the expense of the real one. So I'd evaluate marginal value per token, not aggregate lift. Often the first ten percent of a synthetic dataset gives you most of the benefit and the remaining ninety percent is diluting your signal.

And the third piece, which people underweight, is checking whether it degrades the things you didn't target. Diversity collapse is the classic failure. The generator has its own stylistic fingerprint and its own blind spots, and if you train hard enough on it, the student inherits both. So part of evaluating value is measuring what you lost, not just what you gained.

If I had to compress it: evaluate synthetic data by what it teaches the model that it couldn't learn otherwise, measured on data the generator never saw, at the margin, with an honest accounting of side effects. Everything else is a proxy, and the proxies are exactly where this goes wrong.

r001.rationale: It contrasts judging synthetic data by realism or quality filters with judging it by whether training on it improves the model on relevant held-out tasks.

r002.rationale: It discusses marginal value per token and diminishing returns, but does not identify increasing information density as a way to provide more value from less data.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to evaluate synthetic data by what it helps the model do, rather than by how realistic the data looks. A dataset can look very convincing and still teach the model nothing new—or even reinforce its mistakes.

So I’d start with a controlled comparison: train with and without the synthetic data, keep the training budget comparable, and evaluate on held-out real-world tasks. Does it improve accuracy? Does it help with rare cases? Does it make the model more robust? And do those gains come at the expense of other capabilities?

Then I’d look at the marginal value. If you keep adding synthetic data, are you still getting improvements, or are you mostly repeating patterns the model already knows? Compare that with spending the same resources on collecting or labeling real data.

Ultimately, the value is the improvement you can reliably demonstrate on the tasks you care about, relative to the cost of generating, filtering, and training on that data.

r001.rationale: It says to evaluate synthetic data by what it helps the model do rather than how realistic it looks.

r002.rationale: It discusses marginal gains and repeated patterns, but does not identify increasing information density as a way to give models more value from less data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to evaluate synthetic data through what it does to the model, rather than how convincing the data looks on its own. A dataset can look very polished and still teach the model very little—or reinforce mistakes it already makes.

So I’d start with a controlled comparison: train with and without the synthetic data, keeping the training budget comparable, and evaluate on held-out real data. Does it improve the capabilities we care about? Does it help on unfamiliar cases? Does it introduce regressions? And we need to make sure the evaluation examples haven’t leaked into the generation process.

Then I’d look at the marginal value. If you add another batch of synthetic data, are you still getting improvements, or are you mostly adding repetition? Compare that with spending the same budget on collecting real data or improving the existing data.

Ultimately, the value isn’t the number of examples you generate. It’s the measurable improvement you get per unit of cost, for the particular model and task.

r001.rationale: It contrasts how convincing synthetic data looks with what it does for the model, and recommends measuring its effect on model performance.

r002.rationale: It discusses marginal gains, repetition, and cost, but does not identify increasing information density as a way to provide more value from less data.
